The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK GAP (book p.65, VSAQ 7): the printed answer is one line and never says that the solute must be NON-VOLATILE, never gives ΔTb = Kb m, never gives the unit K kg mol⁻¹, and never says that Kb is a property of the SOLVENT alone. All four are written here. The value Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹ for water is added from the standard data table; it is not printed in this book. NOTATION: Kb is written with a plain small b because Unicode has no subscript b.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The ebullioscopic constant, Kb, is the
elevation of boiling point produced when
one mole of a non-volatile solute is
dissolved in 1000 g (one kilogram) of the
It is also called the molal elevation
steps.why: A one molal solution is one mole of solute in one kilogram of solvent, so the definition is simply the value of ΔTb at m = 1. Fixing the amount this way turns Kb into a fixed number for each solvent, which is what makes the constant usable in a calculation.
common_mistakes: Writing 1000 g of SOLUTION. The definition uses 1000 g of solvent, which is a one molal solution.
Leaving out "non-volatile". A volatile solute adds its own vapour pressure, and then the boiling point does not simply rise.
steps.memory_tip: Ebullioscopic goes with ebullition, which means boiling. So Kb is the boiling point constant.
steps.margin_note: "One mole in 1000 g of solvent" is the marked phrase. The words molal elevation constant are the accepted second name.

steps.label: The equation and the unit
lines: Unit of Kb: K kg mol⁻¹
Kb is a property of the solvent alone. It
does not depend on the solute.
For water, Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹.
steps.why: Elevation of boiling point is a colligative property, so ΔTb depends only on the number of solute particles, measured as molality. Kb carries everything that belongs to the solvent — its boiling point and its enthalpy of vaporisation — which is why the same Kb is used whatever solute is dissolved in it.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔTb = Kb M with molarity. The equation uses molality m, because a boiling experiment changes the temperature and so changes any volume.
Giving the unit as K alone. Kb is ΔTb divided by molality, so the unit is K kg mol⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Kb is fixed by the solvent, so the same 0.52 is used for every solute in water.
steps.margin_note: The unit K kg mol⁻¹ and the "property of the solvent" line are what lift this from a copied sentence to a full answer.

insider_note: Kb and Kf are asked as a pair. Both are properties of the SOLVENT alone, and stating that once in each answer is the line that most scripts leave out.
